---
title: Read predictions
description: "Run the saved model on request files, find each probability, and keep the identifiers you need to act on it."
---

For the supervised payment models, a new request keeps the input fields
and omits the dispute outcomes that are still unknown. This page
scores the flat model saved in [Your first model](your-first-model.qmd),
whose output is small enough to read whole, then the history model saved in
[Train and save](train-and-save.qmd), whose output has one result per
transaction. These are separate artifacts with different input schemas.

## Score the first model

The [first model](your-first-model.qmd) reads `amount` and `merchant`. The
request file keeps those columns, omits `disputed`, and carries an identifier
to join the answer back. Supply a unique application `payment_id` for each
decision row; the examples on this page retain and read that column:

```yaml
payment_id: payment-42
amount: 84.50
merchant: North Market
```

Load the fitted flat-payment artifact and score your application's request
file, retaining the identifier alongside each result:

```python
import relflow as rf

flat_model = rf.Model.load("artifacts/payment-flat.rf")
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="payments/flat/requests.parquet",
    retain=("payment_id",),
)
flat_result = flat_model.predict(datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

`devices=1` collects one Arrow table on one device. `retain` copies the named
source columns into an `inputs` column; nothing else from the request is
echoed. One row of the result has this shape, with placeholders for the
numbers:

```yaml
inputs:
  payment_id: payment-42
predictions:
  disputed:
    state:
      valued: <probability>
      "null": <probability>
      padded: <probability>
      masked: <probability>
      other: <probability>
    content:
      probability: <probability of true>
    inferred: true
```

`content.probability` is the model's estimated dispute probability. Check
its [calibration](evaluation.qmd#check-probability-calibration) before treating
scores as observed dispute rates. `state` predicts whether the value is
valued, null, padded, masked, or other; both `true` and `false` are valued
Booleans. These states describe how a value is represented; see
[value states](../datatypes/index.qmd#value-state). `inferred` marks that this
position was requested as a prediction; it is not a confidence. To read the
probabilities as Python values:

```python
rows = flat_result.to_pylist()
probabilities = {
    row["inputs"]["payment_id"]: row["predictions"]["disputed"]["content"]["probability"]
    for row in rows
}
```

## Score the transaction model

The [transaction model](add-transaction-history.qmd) predicts every retained
transaction. The request keeps the `trxns` records, cut at the decision time
as in [Prepare observations](prepare-observations.qmd), and omits
`disputed` from each one. Add the application's `transaction_id` to each
transaction so each result can be matched to the event it scores:

```yaml
payment_id: payment-42
trxns:
  - transaction_id: trxn-40
    booked_at: "2026-05-21T10:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
  - transaction_id: trxn-41
    booked_at: "2026-05-27T18:15:00"
    amount: 56.20
    merchant: North Market
  - transaction_id: trxn-42
    booked_at: "2026-05-28T14:30:00"
    amount: 84.50
    merchant: North Market
```

Load the history artifact and score the history request file. The application
identifiers are not model fields. Retaining `trxns` keeps its source records
alongside the predictions so their identifiers remain available:

```python
history_model = rf.Model.load("artifacts/payment-history.rf")
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="payments/history/requests.parquet",
    retain=("payment_id", "trxns"),
)
result = history_model.predict(datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

This result contains `predictions.trxns`, a list with one result per retained
transaction in request order. Each item carries the same `disputed` payload
as above:

```python
observation = result.slice(0, 1).to_pylist()[0]
probabilities = [
    transaction["disputed"]["content"]["probability"]
    for transaction in observation["predictions"]["trxns"]
]
```

The list is as long as the retained history, not the branch cap: a request
with three transactions gets three results. With `overflow="tail"` and more
than 32 transactions, only the last 32 are retained and scored. The source
records under `inputs.trxns` still contain the full processed request list.
For this model's tail policy, match the predictions to the same last 32
records:

```python
retained_transactions = observation["inputs"]["trxns"][-32:]
transaction_probabilities = {
    transaction["transaction_id"]: probability
    for transaction, probability in zip(retained_transactions, probabilities, strict=True)
}
```

The latest payment's probability is `probabilities[-1]`. This is the score to
compare with the flat model when evaluating the same latest-payment decisions.

## Read many rows at once

Converting to Python objects is fine for a few rows. For offline analysis of
a whole request file, keep the table columnar and let Polars flatten the
nesting. Keep the same tail of source transaction identifiers alongside the
predictions and explode both lists together: each
`explode` turns a list into rows and each `unnest` turns a struct into
columns, following the record's shape from the outside in:

```python
import polars as pl

transactions = (
    pl.from_arrow(result)
    .select(
        pl.col("inputs").struct.field("payment_id"),
        (
            pl.col("inputs")
            .struct.field("trxns")
            .list.tail(32)
            .list.eval(pl.element().struct.field("transaction_id"))
            .alias("transaction_id")
        ),
        pl.col("predictions").struct.field("trxns"),
    )
    .explode("transaction_id", "trxns")
    .unnest("trxns")
    .unnest("disputed")
    .unnest("content")
)
```

`transactions` has one row per scored transaction with `payment_id`,
`transaction_id`, `state`, `probability`, and `inferred` columns, in request
order. This flattened table suits offline analysis or file output. HTTP
serving requires one response row per request observation; the
[decision postprocessor](../guides/postprocessing.qmd) keeps the transaction
results in lists within that row.

## Act on the result

Choosing a threshold is an application decision. A
[postprocessor](../guides/postprocessing.qmd) can turn the nested table into
decision columns while preserving one row per request, for reuse in batch
files and HTTP serving. For large request files, write results as they complete with
[batch inference](../guides/batch-inference.qmd); for online requests, see
[Serving](../guides/serving.qmd).

Two other columns can appear. `representations` holds exported embeddings
when a node has `embed=True`. These expose the trained model's learned
context for separate predictors; see
[Reusable representations](reusable-representations.qmd). Nested targets,
structural nulls, and the full Arrow contract are described in
[Prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd).

Next, [evaluate](evaluation.qmd) the model against the review
process it is meant to support.
